question.text: A 72-year-old man is brought to the physician for the evaluation of severe nosebleeds and two episodes of bloody vomit over the past 40 minutes. He reports that he has had recurrent nosebleeds almost daily for the last 3 weeks. The nosebleeds last between 30 and 40 minutes. He appears pale. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 95/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination of the nose with a speculum does not show an anterior bleeding source. The upper body of this patient is elevated and his head is bent forward. Cold packs are applied and the nose is pinched at the nostrils for 5–10 minutes. Topical phenylephrine is administered. Despite all measures, the nosebleed continues. Anterior and posterior nasal packing is placed, but bleeding persists. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Endoscopic ligation of the sphenopalatine artery
options.B: Endoscopic ligation of the posterior ethmoidal artery
options.C: Endoscopic ligation of the anterior ethmoidal artery
options.D: Endoscopic ligation of the lesser palatine artery
options.E: Endoscopic ligation of the greater palatine artery

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with severe, persistent epistaxis despite initial management, including topical vasoconstrictors, anterior and posterior nasal packing, and cold compresses. This suggests a likely source of bleeding that is not easily controlled with standard measures. The persistent bleeding despite these interventions points towards a more complex and potentially vascular source, such as the sphenopalatine artery. Endoscopic ligation of the sphenopalatine artery is the most appropriate next step to address this.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Persistent bleeding despite anterior and posterior nasal packing and topical vasoconstrictors.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other options might be considered in certain scenarios, the persistent bleeding despite standard measures makes the sphenopalatine artery the most likely culprit. The other arteries are less likely to be the primary source of such severe, refractory bleeding.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has persistent nosebleeds despite standard measures, suggesting a source beyond the anterior nasal passages. The persistent bleeding despite packing and phenylephrine indicates a likely source in the posterior nasal space. The greater palatine artery is a major posterior nasal artery that supplies blood to the posterior wall of the nasal cavity and is a common site for chronic posterior nosebleeds. The sphenopalatine artery (option A) is more likely to be involved in acute hemorrhage, while the lesser palatine artery (option D) is typically not a major source of chronic bleeding. The ethmoidal arteries (options B and C) are more commonly involved in anterior bleeds, which have been excluded by speculum examination. Therefore, endoscopic ligation of the greater palatine artery (option E) is the most appropriate next step.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Persistent bleeding despite standard measures and anterior speculum examination
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered an anterior source (ruled out by speculum exam), hypertension (ruled out by low BP), coagulopathy (not indicated by bleeding despite cold packs and phenylephrine), and other systemic causes (not indicated by other symptoms). The most likely diagnosis is a posterior nasal artery aneurysm or chronic posterior epistaxis.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient has persistent posterior epistaxis despite anterior packing and topical agents, indicating a posterior source. The sphenopalatine artery is the most common source of posterior epistaxis and is accessible via endoscopic ligation. Other options target less common or anterior vessels, which are less likely to be the source given the clinical course.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Persistent bleeding after anterior packing and absence of anterior bleeding source on speculum exam strongly suggests posterior epistaxis, most commonly from the sphenopalatine artery.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other causes like coagulopathy or systemic disease were not ruled out, but the persistent posterior bleeding makes vascular ligation the next step. Anterior vessels (B, C, E) are less likely given the posterior bleeding pattern; D (lesser palatine) is typically associated with posterior oropharyngeal bleeding, not nasal.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Severe, persistent bleeding despite nasal packing and medical measures, in an elderly patient with no visible source on exam
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other vascular sources (B, C, D, E) are less likely as the sphenopalatine artery is the main vascular supply of the nasal mucosa. Endoscopic evaluation is standard for persistent bleeding after failed packing. Ethmoid or palatine artery ligation would be secondary to controlling the sphenopalatine first.
